source.title: An Open-Source Training Dataset for Foundation Models for Black-box Optimization
source.authors: Aaron Klein; Herilalaina Rakotoarison; Luca Thale-Bombien; David Salinas

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates compute-scaling behavior in decoder-only transformer foundation models trained on black-box optimization trajectories, a different domain and data type from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper directly reports a power-law fit between held-out validation loss and compute, and an extrapolation to its largest configuration. The optimizer-imitation comparisons also report how evaluation performance changes with model size and token budget. References to scaling-law results from other work are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: The authors train decoder-only transformers (2M–80M parameters, 200M–2B tokens) on tokenized black-box-optimization trajectories. They fit held-out validation loss against compute as a power law, check extrapolation to a held-out largest configuration (Fig. 4), and compare optimizer-imitation quality across model sizes and token budgets (Figs. 5–6). This is a new, non-text setting with its own results on the claim's power-law form, extrapolation and scale-driven downstream improvement.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that validation loss versus compute is well captured by a power law that extrapolates to their largest (80M, 2B-token) run. The exponent is much shallower than in LLMs, so compute gains are modest. Their main conclusion is broader: pretraining on BBO-Pile lets transformers imitate black-box optimizers, with closer imitation at larger model sizes and token budgets (above about 1B tokens). Imitation is weaker on unseen global-optimization search spaces.
record.recipe_differences: It fits validation loss against combined compute using Pareto-dominant points, rather than measuring natural-language held-out cross-entropy and separately studying parameters, tokens, and compute. The trained systems model black-box optimization trajectories.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports higher stochasticity in validation loss than for LLMs. For optimizer imitation, smaller parameter counts and lower token budgets give weaker matching; a budget below 800M tokens is described as insufficient for fully capturing CQR's sampling distribution.
record.problems: The scaling study covers 2M–80M parameters and 200M–2B tokens and reports a single fitted loss-versus-compute relationship. The authors note higher stochasticity than in LLMs, but do not report uncertainty for the fitted exponent or numerical extrapolation error. The loss improvements are described as modest. The optimizer-imitation outcomes are mostly qualitative in the text, with results shown in plots.
record.rows_left_out: Task-by-task optimizer imitation curves and additional token-budget/model-scale plot outcomes in Figures 5–8 and Appendix G were not separately extracted; the paper describes many as plots, and the main text gives only the aggregate or illustrative qualitative outcomes recorded above.

untested.parts: All of it. There is no natural-language pretraining. The only loss fit is for non-text trajectory models (recorded under V5), and there are no separate parameter-only or token-only power-law fits.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude; only a short (<10x compute) extrapolation to one held-out run is shown, with no numeric error.
All. Fig. 4 marks a 'compute-optimal frontier', but no allocation exponents for N or D are estimated.
All. Depth and width vary across sizes (Table 3) but are confounded with parameter count.
Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes; power-law form over more than about two orders of compute; separate N and D laws.
Quantitative predictability: no mapping from loss or scale to imitation quality is fitted; language-model benchmarks are not tested.
All. There is no comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting, schedules or data choices.

missing.what: Final validation loss for every (N, D, LR, batch) cell, which would allow loss-versus-N at fixed D and loss-versus-D at fixed N. Best cells fall from about 0.88 (2M, 2B) to about 0.81 (80M, 2B). Some 2M/D=1B cells read 0.00, an apparent artifact.
Per-hyperparameter sampling densities align more with the reference optimizer as training progresses (10%→100% of 2B tokens). This is a qualitative token-scaling result on downstream imitation.

record.verdict_notes: I moved r1 from V1 to V5, because the models are trajectory-sequence models, not language models. I removed the reader's V6 limits_scope: the weaker imitation at 2M parameters or below 800M tokens is the scaling trend itself, not a qualification. Scale range is small: 2M–80M params and about two orders of compute. The study is a preprint; code, data and checkpoints are stated to be released (the record said 'not stated').

versions.untested_parts: Natural-language pretraining and separate parameter-only or token-only loss scaling are not tested; the reported fit relates validation loss to combined compute in black-box optimization models.
Extrapolation is reported for the largest configuration in this study, not for language models or a broader set of independently held-out large runs.
The study does not estimate compute-optimal parameter and token allocations or their growth rates.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count is reported.
The tested setting is black-box optimization trajectory training; image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
The evaluation concerns imitation of black-box optimizers, not language-model downstream benchmarks or a quantitative mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance.
The study does not systematically vary fit methods, parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, or data to test how these choices change scaling exponents or allocation trends.

rows.subject: decoder-only transformer models for black-box optimization
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained on optimizer trajectories; 200M to 2B tokens
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss as a function of compute using Pareto-dominant points from the validation curves.
rows.note: The authors describe the relationship as well captured by a power law. They note higher stochasticity than for LLMs and describe loss improvements from increasing compute as modest.
rows.check: Unlinked from V1. V1 names held-out pretraining loss of language models, while these models learn optimizer-trajectory strings. This is the non-text setting V5 covers. The fit spans only about 1e16–1e18 FLOPs (about two orders) and loss about 0.91→0.84. The exponent is 0.0157, which the authors call shallower than LLMs', and there is no uncertainty on the fit.

rows.subject: 80M-parameter model trained on 2B tokens
rows.stage_stated: pre-trained on optimizer trajectories for 2B tokens
rows.operation_detail: Compare the power-law fit from smaller Pareto-dominant validation-curve points with the largest configuration.
rows.value: The authors state that the fit extrapolates accurately to the largest configuration.
rows.note: The largest configuration is identified as 80M parameters trained on 2B tokens; no numerical prediction error is stated.
rows.check: The extrapolation target (80M, 2B tokens; about 1e18 FLOPs) is less than one order of magnitude beyond the fitted points, not 'orders of magnitude larger'. No numeric prediction error is given; 'extrapolates accurately' is the authors' words read off Fig. 4.

rows.subject: models selected from the scaling grid
rows.operation_detail: Compare how well models at different parameter scales imitate optimizer behavior on evaluation tasks.
rows.value: The authors report that 2M parameters are insufficient to fully match CQR, particularly during early iterations; performance is matched more closely with larger parameter counts.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation over 30 runs are shown in Figure 5; no numeric values stated in the text.
rows.note: Outcome is reported qualitatively in the text; the plotted curves are not transcribed as numerical values.
rows.check: State changed from partial. The row reports the scaling effect itself: imitation matches CQR more closely as parameters grow, and the 2M shortfall is the low end of that trend. The evidence is qualitative only (plots); no predictive relation to scale or loss is fitted.

rows.subject: 80M-parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Compare optimizer imitation across token budgets.

conditions.value: unseen TabRepo CatBoost Fashion-MNIST search space

rows.measure: ability to capture CQR's sampling distribution and optimizer performance
rows.value: A token budget below 800M appears insufficient to fully capture the CQR sampling distribution.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation over 30 runs are shown in Figure 6; no numeric values stated in the text.
rows.note: The authors give this as an example of weaker imitation at lower token budgets.
rows.check: State changed from partial. The sub-800M shortfall is the low-budget half of the same token-scaling trend that r5 records, not a weaker effect. It could be merged with r5. Qualitative only (Fig. 6d).

rows.subject: 80M-parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Compare optimizer imitation across token budgets.
rows.value: The authors report that models trained for >1B tokens closely match the original performance.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation over 30 runs are shown in Figure 6; no numeric values stated in the text.
rows.note: This is the authors' stated aggregate comparison across the plotted token-budget results.
rows.check: This is the high-budget end of the token-scaling trend for the 80M model. Qualitative; no numbers or predictive fit.

relationships.condition: decoder-only transformers trained on BBO optimizer trajectories, 2M–80M params, 200M–2B tokens, about 1e16–1e18 FLOPs
relationships.reason: Validation loss versus compute on Pareto points fits L = 1.6105·C^-0.0157, which the authors call well captured by a power law (r1), and it extrapolates to the held-out largest run (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Pareto-frontier validation loss fits L = 1.6105·C^-0.0157 and extrapolates to the held-out largest run.

relationships.reason: The authors report loss 'higher stochasticity compared to LLMs'. The exponent (0.0157) is far shallower than LLM exponents, so gains are modest (about 0.91→0.84). No fit uncertainty is reported (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Loss decreased from about 0.91 to 0.84 with exponent 0.0157, showing greater stochasticity than LLM losses and no reported fit uncertainty.

relationships.condition: short-range extrapolation (<10x compute) to the single held-out 80M/2B-token run, BBO setting
relationships.reason: The authors state the power law fitted on smaller Pareto points extrapolates accurately to the largest configuration; no numeric error is given (r2).
relationships.display_finding: The fitted power law reportedly accurately predicted the held-out 80M model trained on 2B tokens, less than 10× beyond the fitting compute.

relationships.condition: optimizer-imitation fidelity (CQR/RS trajectories) as parameters (2M→80M) and tokens (200M→2B, 80M model) increase; qualitative, from plots
relationships.reason: Imitation matches the original optimizer more closely with more parameters (r3) and with token budgets above 1B versus below 800M (r4, r5). The improvement is directional, not shown to be quantitatively predictable.
relationships.display_finding: Imitation fidelity improved with model size and with token budgets above 1B versus below 800M, without testing quantitative predictability.
